name: Valeeswarar Temple, Kuranganilmuttam
deity: Shiva as Valeeswarar, with the Goddess Iraiyar Valaiyammai
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Sambandar (7th century); a Pallava rock-cut cave nearby, with Rashtrakuta and Chola inscriptions
dynasty: Pallava (nearby cave), with Rashtrakuta and Chola inscriptions
summary: South of Kanchipuram, the village of Kuranganilmuttam takes its name from a monkey, a squirrel and a crow — Vali, Indra and Yama in disguise, who tradition says worshipped Shiva here and were freed from their curses.

sections.history: Thirukkuranganilmuttam is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung by Thirugnana Sambandar in the Tevaram. The village lies near the Palar, some 10 km south of Kanchipuram by road, in Tiruvannamalai district. About half a kilometre to the north is a small rock-cut cave shrine, attributed on grounds of style to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I in the early seventh century, though no Pallava inscription has been found there. The village's earliest inscription belongs to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III in the tenth century and records a gift of land, calling the place part of Pallavapuram; the name Tirukkuranganilmuttam itself first appears in an inscription of Kulothunga III.
sections.architecture: The Valeeswarar temple is a modest village shrine of the Dravidian tradition, with the sanctum of the Lord and a separate shrine of the goddess Iraiyar Valaiyammai. Sculpted panels show the monkey, the squirrel and the crow at worship, recalling the legend in the village's name. The nearby Pallava cave, known locally as the Kal Mandakam, is a simple pillared hall cut into the rock, one of the early experiments in stone of the Pallava age.
sections.legends: The name joins three Tamil words: kurangu, the monkey; anil, the squirrel; and muttam, taken here as the crow. The sthala purana tells that Vali, the monkey king, worshipped Shiva here at the entrance, Indra in the form of a squirrel from the south, and Yama as a crow from the north; each, bearing a curse, was released by the Lord's grace. The pond called Kaakkai Madu is said to have been made when Yama, as a crow, pierced the earth with his beak to draw water for worship.
sections.festivals: Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri and Karthigai Deepam are kept with special worship, with the festivals of the goddess through the year. As at most village shrines, dates and processions vary; confirm locally.
sections.experience: Kuranganilmuttam is a quiet village shrine, easily joined to a visit to Kanchipuram. Pilgrims look for the panels of the three creatures at worship, walk to the Kaakkai Madu, and many go on to the Pallava cave north of the village, a reminder of how old the sacred life of this countryside is.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Kuranganilmuttam lies about 10 km south of Kanchipuram, across the Palar, reached by road by way of Dusi (Thoosi) on the Kanchipuram–Vandavasi road. Kanchipuram is the nearest railway station and town; Chennai International Airport, about 80 km away, is the nearest airport.
